Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Gabon predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording. Multiple studies confirm that health facilities, including clinics, collect data manually in registers, with data managers later aggregating and entering it into national systems like DHIS2 (launched nationally in 2024) or SNIS at district or regional levels. A 2022 JMIR pilot study explicitly states that facilities are compelled to use paper records due to inadequate digital infrastructure, making point-of-care electronic recording challenging. Recent evaluations (2022) show only 45% of structures have digital tools for data collection, with many lacking consultation registers entirely. National e-health initiatives (eGabon/SNIS since 2016, DHIS2 2024) focus on centralized aggregation, not routine point-of-service digital capture in rural areas. Pilots like Routine Info exist but are limited to select facilities and not scaled to most rural clinics. Barriers include poor internet outside cities, fragmented systems, low digital capacity, and medical desertification in rural zones. While national policy pushes digitalization, rural reality remains paper-dominant with digital limited to upward reporting, fitting score 1.

revision_notes: Confirmed. The 2022 JMIR pilot study (fetched and read) documents that Gabonese health facilities are compelled to use paper registers owing to inadequate digital infrastructure, with data managers manually transcribing paper entries into DHIS2 at district/regional level rather than capturing data digitally at the point of care. A companion data-quality survey of 71 health facilities (fieldwork 2019, published 2023) found only 45% possessed any digital tool for data collection/storage, and only 42% met all criteria for capturing and preserving data - and this sample was concentrated in the Libreville-Owendo and West regions, i.e. more urbanised areas than rural Gabon, meaning rural facilities are likely to be even more paper-reliant. DHIS2 was launched nationally in December 2024 but operates at the aggregation/reporting level, not facility point-of-care capture. No evidence was found of routine digital data capture in rural clinics specifically. Score 1 stands. One of the three originally-cited sources (PMC7444076) was blocked by an anti-bot check and jelsciences.com returned a 403 error, so these could not be directly re-verified; the JMIR study (PMC9587495) was successfully fetched and supports the score independently.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Gabon record patient data on paper at the point of care. A 2022 JMIR pilot study found that facilities are compelled to use paper registers owing to inadequate digital infrastructure (unreliable connectivity, limited computer access), and a national data-quality assessment of 71 health facilities found that only 45% possessed any digital tool for data collection and storage, with data managers subsequently transcribing paper register entries into national platforms such as DHIS2 (launched nationally in December 2024) for aggregated reporting. Digitalisation therefore remains concentrated at the aggregation and reporting level rather than at the facility point of care, particularly in rural areas where infrastructure constraints are most acute.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Gabon predominantly use paper-based recording for criminal cases and complaints. A February 2026 government announcement detailed new digital tools like FARIAJ (automated judicial antecedents database) for identity checks and SITA for promotions, aimed at national police efficiency.Ministère de l'Intérieur. However, no evidence indicates deployment at rural point-of-service; these appear centralized/national. A March 2026 APT roundtable on standardized custody registers confirmed current paper-based systems as the baseline, with infrastructure limits in remote areas hindering even paper standardization, and digitalization discussed only as future aspiration.APT. Police complaints site promotes fillable PDF forms requiring in-person validation, suggesting manual processes.FPN. Key barriers: poor rural infrastructure, training gaps, electricity/connectivity issues. National digital ambitions (e.g., Digital Gabon project) exist but gap with rural reality persists, limited to pilots/central use.

Score 1 stands for rural police stations specifically.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Gabon rely on paper-based recording for criminal cases, complaints and custody records. A February 2026 national roundtable on standardised custody registers, convened by the Ministry of Justice and the Association for the Prevention of Torture, confirms that current record-keeping in police stations and gendarmerie brigades is paper-based, with digitalisation of custody records discussed only as a future ambition and infrastructure limitations flagged as a particular constraint in remote areas. National digitalisation projects announced around the same time, such as the FARIAJ judicial-antecedents database and the SITA promotions system, operate at a centralised level rather than providing point-of-service digital capture. A digital citizen-complaint application launched in May 2026 remains confined to a small number of Libreville neighbourhoods, with rural expansion still pending.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Gabon primarily use paper-based processes for birth registration. Declarations are made to civil registrars within extended timelines (1 month in rural areas per recent law changes), involving manual supplementary judgments from tribunals and transcription into certificates via "One-Stop Centres" in provinces. No evidence found of routine digital recording at point-of-service in rural facilities; processes described as complex administrative/legal without mention of e-CRVS or electronic entry at registries. Digital pilots exist for data collection (e.g., Go-Data app for mapping hard-to-reach populations) and national health info systems are planned, but CRVS remains non-centralized with poor interoperability to HMIS. Barriers include remoteness, low awareness, cultural practices among indigenous groups, coordination gaps, and Covid-19 delays. National policy aims at integration (e.g., registration at health facilities), but rural reality lags with low pickup rates (34%) and focus on late registrations via projects rather than real-time digital point-of-care. High national completeness (~90% in 2012 DHS) masks rural challenges; no specific rural digital evidence post-2012.

revision_notes: Confirmed. Law 008/2022 (Journal Officiel) establishes a legal framework for a digital, biometric, centralised civil registry (etat civil numerique, biometrique et centralise), but this is a legislative aspiration rather than an operational reality. A 2023 ID4Africa/Thales presentation on the IBOGA national identity project explicitly depicts the current ('today') civil registration system as 'paper-based, decentralised', with a centralised digital civil registry positioned as the future ('tomorrow') state once IBOGA is deployed - direct evidence that rural registry offices were not yet digitised as of 2023. UNDP joint-programme reporting corroborates this: rural birth registration relies on manual declarations, tribunal-issued supplementary judgments for late registration, and paper-based provincial 'One-Stop Centres', with no evidence of routine digital point-of-service capture. Score 1 stands. The World Bank publication originally cited (openknowledge.worldbank.org) returned only a bare title with no retrievable content and could not be used as supporting evidence.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Gabon record vital events on paper at the point of registration. Although Law 008/2022 establishes a legal framework for a digital, biometric and centralised civil registry, implementation is still under way: a 2023 national identity project presentation (IBOGA, presented at ID4Africa) depicts the current civil registration system as paper-based and decentralised, with a centralised digital registry positioned as a future state once the project is deployed. Rural birth registration continues to rely on manual declarations to civil registrars, tribunal-issued supplementary judgments for late registrations, and paper processing through provincial One-Stop Centres, with no evidence of routine digital data capture at rural registry offices.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Gabon has implemented SIGE (Système d’Information pour la Gestion de l’Éducation), a digital education management information system for collecting, analyzing, and exploiting educational data, including recent integration of school health indicators Gabon Media Time. Ministry prioritizes strengthening school data collection with World Bank tablets and UNESCO software for field collection, with training ongoing PointNoirTV. UNESCO SDG4 data relies on administrative sources alongside surveys UNESCO SDG4 Profile. No evidence of direct digital recording (e.g., tablets for attendance/grades) at rural primary school level; efforts suggest pilots/district aggregation from paper, fitting score 2. Broader digital Gabon push exists but civil registry remains paper-based analogously World Bank Digital Gabon.

revision_notes: Recalculated from 1 to 2. The Value Code recorded on the row (1, Entirely paper) contradicted the row's own Comments text, which explicitly argued for a score of 2 ('fitting score 2') - this inconsistency has been corrected. Evidence: in March 2025 the Ministry of Education, the World Bank and UNESCO announced provision of tablets and data-collection software to strengthen SIGE-based school data collection, with several establishments already equipped and training under way. By June 2026 a related UNICEF/Airtel digital-education programme had expanded to 146 schools connected nationally (a minority of Gabon's total primary schools), with fifth-grade curricula digitised on the Learning Passport platform, 120 teachers trained, and 140 establishments connected to the internet; earlier reporting confirms this programme has reached at least one explicitly rural school (Oyane 4), though it is oriented mainly towards learning-content delivery rather than administrative record capture. Taken together, this is partial, still-expanding digital data capture concentrated in a minority of schools, consistent with 'mostly paper, some digital' (code 2) rather than 'entirely paper' (code 1); there is no evidence supporting the higher 'mostly digital' (code 3).
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Gabon predominantly rely on paper administrative records, with digital data capture only partially introduced. Since March 2025 the Ministry of National Education, working with the World Bank and UNESCO, has been distributing tablets and data-collection software to strengthen the Systeme d'Information pour la Gestion de l'Education (SIGE), reaching a growing but still minority number of schools nationally by mid-2026 (146 schools connected, fifth-grade curricula digitised via the Learning Passport platform, 120 teachers trained). Separate UNICEF-Airtel digital-learning partnerships have equipped some rural schools, including Oyane 4, with tablets and connectivity, although these programmes are oriented towards learning-content delivery rather than administrative data capture. Overall, digital data capture in rural primary schools remains the exception rather than the rule, with paper records still predominant but digital tools increasingly present.
